title: IPC 1 Entrance Examination Sample – Section A (Reading)
description: AY2027 sample reading section. Read each text and choose the best answer (A–D). 40 questions across three texts. (Section B: Writing is not included because it is not multiple choice.)

passages.title: Text 1: Into the Deep
passages.text:
The deep sea is one of the least explored places on Earth. More than ninety percent of the ocean floor has never been seen by humans, and scientists believe many species remain undiscovered in the darkness below.

One of the strangest creatures in the deep sea is the anglerfish. The female anglerfish has a small glowing organ that hangs in front of her head like a fishing rod. This light attracts smaller fish in the dark water, and when they swim close enough, the anglerfish snaps them up with its enormous jaws.

Pressure in the deep ocean is extreme. At great depths, the water pushes down with a force far greater than at the surface. Despite this, many animals thrive there, including giant squid and certain species of shark.

Scientists use special underwater vehicles called submersibles to explore these depths. Each mission provides new data and often leads to the discovery of previously unknown creatures.

Adapted from “The Deep Ocean” — BBC Earth / BBC Future

passages.title: Text 2: News at the Speed of Light
passages.text:
For most of human history, news spread slowly. A battle in one country might take weeks or months to be known elsewhere. Information moved at the speed of horses, ships, and messengers. Today, a single event can reach billions of people within seconds.

The rise of social media has changed how we receive information. Platforms like Instagram and YouTube allow anyone with internet access to share content instantly. This spread of information to ordinary people is positive in many ways. People can report events as they happen, without relying on traditional editors or broadcasters.

However, speed does not always mean accuracy. False stories often spread faster than true ones because they are more emotional and surprising. A 2018 study from MIT found that false news reached people six times faster than accurate reports. People often share shocking headlines without checking if they are true.

Because of this, media literacy has become an essential skill. Schools in some countries now teach students how to evaluate sources and question information. It is not enough to receive information quickly; people must also learn how to think about it carefully.

Adapted from "The Spread of False News Online" — MIT Media Lab & The Guardian

passages.title: Text 3: What the Stones Remember
passages.text:
There is a particular kind of silence that belongs only to very old places. I first encountered it in the ruins of a stone monastery in the mountains, where the walls, though roofless, still held their shape after seven centuries. Standing among them, I noticed that the noise of the world — traffic, wind, the ordinary hum of being alive — seemed to fall away. What remained was something harder to name.

We tend to think of silence as an absence, a mere emptiness where sound has been removed. But this silence felt different. It had weight. It suggested that something had once happened here, and that the stones, patient and indifferent, had simply continued to exist long after the people were gone. I found myself thinking about what it means to leave something behind — whether a building, a book, or even a habit of kindness passed from one person to another.

Philosophers have often asked what gives a human life its meaning. Many answers have been offered: love, achievement, contribution to something larger than oneself. What struck me in that old place was a quieter possibility — that meaning might not need to be proclaimed or recorded at all. Perhaps it is enough simply to have been present, to have shaped a small corner of the world, and to leave it subtly different from how you found it.

The monastery had no sign explaining its history. Whatever was remembered there was remembered in stone.

Adapted from "Places of Silence" — an essay in the tradition of The Atlantic / Aeon Magazine

questions.question: According to paragraph one, how much of the ocean floor has been seen by humans?
questions.explanation: More than ninety percent has never been seen, so less than ten percent has been seen.

questions.question: Which animal is described in detail in the passage?
questions.explanation: Paragraph two describes the anglerfish and how it hunts.

questions.question: What do scientists use to explore the deep ocean?
questions.explanation: Paragraph four names special underwater vehicles called submersibles.

questions.question: “Attracts” (paragraph two) most nearly means:
questions.explanation: The light brings smaller fish close, so “attracts” means draws toward.

questions.question: “Thrive” (paragraph three) most nearly means:
questions.explanation: “Despite this” signals that animals do well in spite of the pressure.

questions.question: In the sentence “when they swim close enough, the anglerfish snaps them up,” “they” refers to:
questions.explanation: The light attracts smaller fish, and it is those fish that swim close.

questions.question: In the sentence “many animals thrive there,” “there” refers to:
questions.explanation: The paragraph is about extreme pressure in the deep ocean.

questions.question: Why does the anglerfish use a glowing organ?
options: To attract prey in the dark
questions.explanation: The light attracts smaller fish, which the anglerfish then catches.

questions.question: What can be inferred about deep-sea exploration missions?
options: They often lead to new discoveries
They are simple to carry out
They focus only on known animals
questions.explanation: Each mission provides new data and often leads to discoveries of unknown creatures.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of this passage?
options: To warn about dangers in the ocean
To tell a fictional story about sea creatures
To explain how to become a scientist
To inform readers about the deep sea
questions.explanation: The passage presents factual information about the deep sea.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: The deep sea is a harsh but active environment with much still unknown
Anglerfish are the most dangerous creatures in the ocean
The ocean floor has already been mostly explored
questions.explanation: The passage covers extreme conditions, life that thrives there, and how much remains unexplored.

questions.question: According to the passage, all are TRUE EXCEPT:
options: Many deep-sea species have not yet been discovered
Some animals are able to live in extreme pressure
The deep sea has lower pressure than the surface
Scientists use special vehicles to explore deep areas
questions.explanation: Pressure at depth is far greater than at the surface, so option C is false.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best summary of the passage?
options: Scientists have explored most of the ocean and found only a few unusual creatures
The deep sea is an extreme environment where most animals cannot survive
The deep sea remains largely unexplored, and scientists continue to discover new life there
Underwater machines are mainly used to study common ocean animals
questions.explanation: This captures both the unexplored nature of the deep sea and ongoing discovery.

questions.question: According to paragraph one, how long could news take to travel in the past?
questions.explanation: A battle might take weeks or months to be known elsewhere.

questions.question: What did the 2018 MIT study find?
options: True news spreads faster than false news
False news reaches people much faster than true news
questions.explanation: False news reached people six times faster than accurate reports.

questions.question: “This” in “This spread of information to ordinary people…” refers to:
questions.explanation: The preceding sentences describe social media platforms letting anyone share content.

questions.question: “Accuracy” (paragraph three) most nearly means:
questions.explanation: “Speed does not always mean accuracy” contrasts speed with being correct.

questions.question: “Surprising” (paragraph three) most nearly means:
questions.explanation: Surprising things are unexpected.

questions.question: In “think about it carefully,” “it” refers to:
questions.explanation: The sentence is about receiving information and learning to think about that information.

questions.question: Why do false stories often spread faster than true stories?
options: They are more emotional and surprising
questions.explanation: Paragraph three says false stories are more emotional and surprising.

questions.question: What can be inferred about traditional editors and broadcasters?
questions.explanation: People can now report events without relying on them, so their role has lessened.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest is a risk of fast information sharing?
options: People often share information without verifying it
questions.explanation: The passage says people often share shocking headlines without checking if they are true.

questions.question: Why has information spread become much faster today?
options: Anyone can share information instantly online
People read more news than before
questions.explanation: Social media platforms allow anyone with internet access to share content instantly.

questions.question: Why have some schools added media literacy to their curriculum?
options: People need skills to evaluate information
questions.explanation: Schools teach students how to evaluate sources and question information.

questions.question: The writer’s attitude toward social media is best described as:
options: balanced, recognising both benefits and risks
questions.explanation: The writer notes benefits (instant sharing) and risks (false news).

questions.question: According to the passage, all of the following are true EXCEPT:
options: False news can spread faster than true news
Social media allows people to share information instantly
News in the past moved slowly
Media literacy guarantees that all information is accurate
questions.explanation: The passage never claims media literacy guarantees accuracy.

questions.question: What is the main message of the passage?
options: Fast information sharing makes critical thinking more important
questions.explanation: The passage concludes that people must learn to think carefully about information.

questions.question: Which best summarises paragraph four?
options: Schools are entertaining students with media lessons
Media literacy is only important for professional journalists
Some schools now feel it is important to teach media literacy
questions.explanation: Paragraph four says schools in some countries now teach students to evaluate information.

questions.question: In paragraph one, why does the writer say the noise of the world “seemed to fall away”?
options: The place created a feeling of separation from everyday life
The writer could not hear properly
questions.explanation: The phrase conveys a feeling of leaving ordinary life behind, not literal soundproofing.

questions.question: What does the writer imply about the stones in paragraph two?
options: They should be protected as historical objects
They show that places can outlast the people who built them
questions.explanation: The stones continued to exist long after the people were gone.

questions.question: What can be inferred about the writer’s view of memory and history?
options: They can be preserved in physical places without explanation
They must be written down to survive
They exist only in people’s minds
They are not important to understanding the past
questions.explanation: The monastery had no sign, yet “whatever was remembered there was remembered in stone.”

questions.question: “Encountered” (paragraph one) most nearly means:
questions.explanation: The writer came across and experienced the silence.

questions.question: “Indifferent” (paragraph two) most nearly means:
questions.explanation: The stones simply continued to exist without reacting to anything.

questions.question: In “It suggested that something had once happened here,” “It” refers to:
questions.explanation: The preceding sentences describe how this silence “had weight.”

questions.question: How would you best describe the writer’s attitude?
questions.explanation: The tone is thoughtful and contemplative throughout.

questions.question: What is the writer’s main idea about meaning in life in paragraph three?
options: It can come from small, quiet actions
It can only be understood through philosophy
questions.explanation: The writer suggests it may be enough to have been present and shaped a small corner of the world.

questions.question: What is the main function of paragraph one?
options: Describe a personal experience that introduces the main idea
Argue for the preservation of old buildings
questions.explanation: The writer recounts a personal experience that leads into the reflection.

questions.question: All are mentioned as sources of meaning EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Paragraph three lists love, achievement and contribution, but not wealth.

questions.question: What is the overall theme of the passage?
options: Old buildings are more valuable than new ones
Historical places lose meaning without explanation
Quiet actions and presence can create lasting meaning
Silence is always a result of loss
questions.explanation: The essay concludes that simply being present and leaving a small mark can be meaningful.

questions.question: Which is the best summary of the passage?
options: A description of a monastery’s history
A reflection on quiet meaning in life
An explanation of silence in old places
questions.explanation: The essay uses the monastery experience to reflect on meaning in life.
